detail.abstract: Digital marketing strategies often use click-through rates (CTR) as a primary performance metric, yet it may not track the sales outcomes firms care about. This study investigates the disconnect between CTR and conversion through a retailer's large-scale field experiment with over 2.4 million emails across 15 campaigns. By randomizing whether price information was included in the messages, we examine how withholding price information impacts user behavior and sales conversions. Our findings reveal that while withholding prices substantially increases CTR (by 22.3%), we find with high precision that it generates no increase in conversions-either directly, cross-channel, or over a four-month window. Heterogeneous treatment effects reveal two offsetting mechanisms: price obfuscation encourages exploration among less-engaged customers, raising clicks and modestly increasing purchases, whereas price transparency enables self-selection among engaged customers who are more conversion-ready. These findings demonstrate empirically that CTR can mislead businesses about campaign effectiveness, with implications for both digital marketing strategy and consumer protection policy.

detail.abstract: The article explores the implications held by artificial intelligence (AI) for newsrooms in Albania through a qualitative research approach. Utilising 24 semi-structured, in-depth interviews with journalists and editors, media professionals' experiences and perceptions regarding the integration of AI into their practices are studied. The results indicate that AI is employed for information gathering, translation, image verification, and news trend analysis. While identified advantages of AI include time optimisation and improved news quality, challenges persist, such as concerns about information accuracy and scepticism of technology. Journalists stress the need for manual verification and the irreplaceable role of the human factor in information security. The use of AI data to identify audience preferences also demonstrates an increase in the capacity of AI to deliver content that resonates with audiences. It is argued in the study that collaboration between AI and journalists is essential to ensure quality and accuracy in journalism.

affiliations: Universiteit Leiden, eLaw

detail.title: The EU AI Act: The Objectives (and the nature) of the Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Gianclaudio Malgieri, Gloria Gonzàlez Fuster, Alessandro Mantelero, Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna (eds.), The AI Act Thematic Commentary, Hart-Bloomsbury, forthcoming 2026

detail.abstract:
This chapter explains the objectives and legal nature of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act by reading its foundational provision as a guide to the whole instrument. It argues that the Regulation is built around a deliberate dual purpose: improving the functioning of the internal market through harmonised rules for placing AI systems on the market and putting them into service, while ensuring a high level of protection for public interests and fundamental rights. The chapter shows how this duality shapes the Act as a hybrid project that combines market integration with a rights and values-based approach to governance, explicitly engaging with health, safety, democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection.

It then outlines how these objectives are operationalised through a tiered, risk-based regulatory architecture, from prohibitions for unacceptable risk practices, to stringent requirements for high-risk systems, to targeted transparency duties and dedicated rules for general-purpose AI, supported by governance, enforcement and innovation measures such as sandboxes. Finally, the chapter situates the Act in its wider regulatory environment, clarifying its complementarity with existing EU frameworks, including data protection and platform regulation, and explaining how this positioning contributes to its distinct legal character.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Multi-Council AI Collaboration, a novel methodology enabling individual practitioners to systematically access multi-expert problem-solving through structured AI-mediated council embodiment within single AI conversation sessions. The framework addresses critical accessibility barriers in innovation methodology where complex problems benefit from diverse expert perspectives but traditional approaches require either extensive individual expertise or expensive expert team coordination.

The methodology was developed and validated through systematic application of software engineering principles with complete AI collaboration transparency throughout the research process. This transparent development approach demonstrates the framework's practical utility for sophisticated intellectual work while establishing new standards for AI-assisted methodology development.

The methodology integrates collective intelligence principles with systematic AI collaboration, enabling practitioners to engage with AI-embodied expert councils representing distinct knowledge domains relevant to their specific challenges. Through structured dialogue protocols and creative synthesis processes, individuals can generate comprehensive multi-perspective solutions while preserving human agency and creative control throughout the problem-solving process.

A proof-of-concept application to organizational AI adoption challenges demonstrates the methodology's practical utility. The framework guided systematic exploration through specialized councils including Strategic Innovation (market analysis, competitive positioning), Human-Centered Design & Well-Being (psychological safety, change management), Technical Implementation (infrastructure, integration), and Governance & Ethics (risk management, compliance). This application produced comprehensive implementation strategies addressing technical, human, and organizational dimensions simultaneously.

The methodology represents convergence innovation at the intersection of design thinking, collective intelligence, and human-AI collaboration. It provides immediate practical utility for individual practitioners, consultants, and resource-constrained organizations while establishing a foundation for future empirical validation studies. Results suggest significant potential for democratizing access to multi-expert problem-solving across domains including strategic planning, policy development, and innovation challenges requiring integrated multi-perspective analysis.

detail.abstract: Digital mental health technologies (DMHTs) now include smartphone apps, web platforms, conversational agents, and sensor-based systems that support assessment, prevention, and treatment of mental health conditions across diverse settings. However, regulatory frameworks in many jurisdictions still treat DMHTs primarily as static products, even though these systems function as evolving services and socio-technical relationships that change over time in response to users, data, and environments. This mismatch complicates classification, evidence generation, and post-market oversight, especially as AI-enabled and adaptive DMHTs become more common in clinical and non-clinical contexts. Drawing on cross-jurisdictional developments in India, the EU/UK, and the United States, as well as conceptual work on generative-AI trust dynamics, this paper argues that the most significant regulatory hurdle for DMHTs is the tension between static product logic and dynamic service reality. It proposes a Δ4 lens for distinguishing "normal maintenance" from "significant change" in DMHTs: changes in (1) intended purpose, (2) clinical impact and harm potential, (3) target population and context, and (4) the algorithmic engine (data and model behavior). The Δ4 lens is illustrated using a scenario in which a digital cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) app adds a clinician-facing risk-prediction dashboard, mapped against guidance from MHRA's 2025 digital mental health technology (DMHT) document, EU MDCG 2020-3, and FDA software-change guidance. The paper further introduces risk-tiered assurance lanes and purpose envelopes as pragmatic design tools to support lifecycle-oriented oversight across jurisdictions, aligned with WHO digital health recommendations, NHS's Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC), and India's emerging Software as a medical device (SaMD) guidance. It concludes with a research and policy agenda for WHO and national regulators to treat DMHTs as evolving socio-technical systems, reducing trust risks where user confidence collapses after invisible failure points.

title: Market Power at Sea: Micro Evidence, Macro Implications
affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics, Kedge Business School Bordeaux, NHH Norwegian School of Economics and University of Nantes

detail.title: Market Power at Sea: Micro Evidence, Macro Implications
detail.abstract: We separate the effects of market power and capacity constraints in transportation. A simple model shows imperfect competition—not capacity constraints—generates differential freight price changes across buyers following a demand shock. Consistent with this, difference-in-differences estimates reveal, after COVID-19 demand surge, freight forwarders faced a 30 pp larger increase in base freight rates than direct shippers despite identical contract terms. This reflects rising carrier markups that disproportionately burden smaller firms and explain at least 35% of freight price growth and 16% of U.S. import price inflation. Thus, competition in transportation is crucial for supplychain resilience and macroeconomic stability

title: How AI Reshapes Human Content Creation: The Case of Grokipedia vs Wikipedia
affiliations: Wake Forest University - Department of Economics and Wake Forest University, Department of Economics

detail.title: How AI Reshapes Human Content Creation: The Case of Grokipedia vs Wikipedia
detail.abstract: Generative AI models rely on large volumes of user-generated content (UGC), yet we know little about how AI tools affect the production of that underlying content. We study this question using the introduction of Grokipedia, an AI-generated online encyclopedia operated by xAI, which provides automated summaries that could either substitute for human editing or expand visibility and draw in new contributors. Using a new panel dataset covering 1.4 million Wikipedia pages of notable individuals-linking edit histories, traffic data, article characteristics, and Grokipedia coverage-we estimate the causal effect of AI summaries on subsequent human contributions by constructing matched samples of treated and untreated pages within occupational fields. We find a consistent and surprising result: the availability of Grokipedia increases human editing activity. Page views also rise, suggesting that AI summaries act as an attention amplifier that ultimately stimulates UGC. We assess how Grokipedia interacts with existing content by constructing a semantic similarity measure between each Grokipedia summary and its corresponding Wikipedia page. Similarity scores are concentrated near one-about 23% of summaries are nearly identical-but exhibit substantial variation. We use this variation to test whether more novel AI summaries elicit greater human engagement, and find that pages with lower similarity experience larger increases in editing after Grokipedia's launch. Our findings show that embedded AI tools can complement-rather than crowd out-voluntary human contributions, highlighting a positive feedback loop between AI features and the data ecosystem that sustains modern AI models.

title: Minimum Resale Price Maintenance in the Absence of Point-of-Sale Service, Agency or Free-Rider Problems
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Business Economics & Public Policy, Chapman University - Economic Science Institute and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR)

detail.title: Minimum Resale Price Maintenance in the Absence of Point-of-Sale Service, Agency or Free-Rider Problems
detail.abstract: We show that MRPM can increase manufacturer profits and total output even in the absence of traditional justifications based on point-of-sale services, retailer effort, or free-riding. The key insight is that MRPM mitigates channel conflict by altering how retailers balance extracting surplus from loyal customers and competing for price-sensitive shoppers. When a manufacturer optimally chooses a wholesale price and MRPM policy, this can intensify competition and create systematic distributional effects: prices fall for loyal consumers but rise for shoppers, and the profits of smaller, shopper-dependent retailers decline. We characterize the conditions under which MRPM raises output, benefits a majority of consumers, and reallocates surplus among the manufacturer, retailers, and different consumer segments. The model helps explain why the political economy of MRPM varies across jurisdictions: even when it increases output, it creates predictable winners and losers, and there is no guarantee that the median consumer or retailer - or the median voter - benefits when minimum resale prices are imposed. These results suggest that the welfare and distributional effects of MRPM are inherently context-dependent and that its legal evaluation is best approached through a rule-of-reason framework that accounts for demand structure, retailer asymmetries, and the composition of consumer types.

title: All Eyes on the Nerd? The Unequal Distribution of Teachers’ Attention
affiliations: , Monash University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: All Eyes on the Nerd? The Unequal Distribution of Teachers’ Attention
detail.abstract: Teachers play a central role in shaping how students benefit from peers, yet little is known about how classroom composition affects their attention-allocation decisions. We conduct a large-scale randomized experiment using realistic class- room vignettes to assess how teachers engage with students under varying scenarios and objectives. The presence of a high achiever reduces the likelihood that teachers engage with a low achiever by about 8%, with substantially larger effects when teachers prioritize task success, consistent with convenience-based decision-making. Using administrative data, we show that low achievers per- form worse when quasi-randomly assigned to a classroom with an exceptional student.

title: MARKETING INTELLIGENCE AND GREEN DECISION-MAKING: DO THEY LEAD TO SUSTAINABLE CONSUMER LOYALTY?

detail.title: MARKETING INTELLIGENCE AND GREEN DECISION-MAKING: DO THEY LEAD TO SUSTAINABLE CONSUMER LOYALTY?
detail.abstract: PurposeThis study investigates the influence of marketing intelligence (MI) and green decision-making (GDM) on sustainable consumer loyalty (SCL) among firms in Calabar South, Nigeria. It explores how intelligence-driven insights and environmentally responsible decisions jointly foster consumer trust and long-term loyalty in emerging markets.Design/methodology/approachA quantitative survey design was employed, targeting 300 business operators, marketing managers, and sales executives across SMEs and service-oriented firms. Data were gathered using the Marketing Intelligence and Green Decision-Making Questionnaire (MIGDM-Q) and analyzed with SPSS and AMOS.FindingsResults revealed that MI (β = 0.682, p < 0.05, R2 = 0.465) and GDM (β = 0.654, p < 0.05, R2 = 0.428) significantly influenced SCL. Firms exhibiting higher MI capabilities and authentic green practices achieved stronger consumer advocacy and repeat patronage.Research limitations/implicationsThe study was limited to a single geographic location and relied on self-reported data, which may affect generalizability. Future research could adopt longitudinal or cross-regional designs to enhance external validity.Practical implicationsManagers should integrate sustainability insights into marketing intelligence systems, enhance transparency, and align strategic decisions with eco-ethical values to strengthen consumer loyalty.Social implicationsThe findings underscore the societal benefits of aligning business intelligence with green responsibility—encouraging environmentally conscious consumer behavior and contributing to sustainable community development.Originality/valueThis study advances consumer marketing discourse by positioning MI and GDM as complementary strategic levers for building sustainable consumer loyalty and ethical brand relationships in developing economies.

title: Superstar Teams
affiliations: University of Cambridge

detail.title: Superstar Teams
detail.abstract: Production increasingly requires specialized expertise. To study the macroeconomic implications, I develop a tractable theory in which firms assemble teams of workers with heterogeneous task-specific skills. Deriving the firm’s production function from optimal task assignment shows that output is maximized when coworkers excel at different tasks yet possess similar overall talent. Crucially, greater skill specificity, while raising potential productivity, endogenously amplifies talent complementarities, i.e., the productivity loss from talent mismatch. This promotes talent concentration into select firms with “superstar teams,” though search frictions prevent perfect sorting. Using German panel micro data, I document industry patterns consistent with this mechanism and calibrate the model. The quantified model shows that, first, growing skill specificity since the mid-1980s has amplified sorting, explaining a significant share of the widely documented “firming up of inequality”. Second, “Smithian” productivity gains from specialization are muted when labor market frictions impede the matching of coworkers with complementary expertise.

detail.abstract: This chapter explores learning culture as a distinctive organizational paradigm that prizes continuous improvement, feedback, curiosity and adaptability. It traces the theoretical lineage of learning culture from the scholarship of Senge, Argyris and Garvin to its modern manifestations in psychological safety, agile learning and growth mindset practices. The chapter examines how organizations such as Microsoft, Pixar and IDEO have embedded learning as a strategic and cultural foundation, analyzes the leadership behaviors and governance structures that sustain it, and considers how learning cultures evolve over time. While highlighting the advantages of innovation, resilience, and engagement, the discussion also acknowledges risks such as analysis paralysis and misalignment between learning and execution. The chapter concludes by offering tools for diagnosing and strengthening learning cultures and by considering how emerging technologies, remote work and artificial intelligence will reshape the pursuit of collective learning in the years ahead.

detail.abstract: This working paper investigates the fundamental role of communication and semiotics in shaping and analyzing the behavioral impacts of digital gambling platforms ("Bets") on consumers. Moving beyond simple economic models, the study employs a sophisticated theoretical framework that integrates Charles Sanders Peirce's triadic model of the sign with Algirdas Julien Greimas's Semiotic Square. This integrated approach allows for the deconstruction of the complex persuasive architecture of digital betting interfaces. We hypothesize that these platforms function as sophisticated meaning-making engines, systematically deploying iconic and indexical sign systems to reduce cognitive friction and accelerate wagering, while utilizing the semiotic square's narrative axes to ideologically reframe financial risk and loss as acceptable entertainment. The paper formulates five core hypotheses regarding the semiotic hierarchy, risk management, communication efficacy, sponsorship legitimacy, and consumer dissatisfaction. This work sets the groundwork for future empirical research, emphasizing the need for critical intervention in the semiotic architecture of digital gambling to inform regulatory, educational, and harm-reduction strategies.

detail.abstract: This case study examines the transformation of a multinational professional services firm, Ardent Advisory, as it transitions from a traditional expertise-driven model to a dynamic learning culture grounded in humility, curiosity, and continuous improvement. Faced with market volatility, knowledge obsolescence, and shifting client expectations, Ardent's leaders recognized that projecting certainty was no longer sufficient. Under the guidance of Managing Partner Isabella Morante, the firm embarked on a cultural reinvention that redefined learning as a collective professional competency and curiosity as a form of expertise. The narrative traces the introduction of feedback-based practices-Learning Loops, Insight Forums, and mentoring systems-that embedded reflection into daily operations while reframing mistakes as sources of insight. Over time, Ardent's "know-it-all" identity evolved into a "learn-it-all" ethos that strengthened innovation, engagement, and client trust. Yet the case also exposes the risks of overreflection and cultural drift, illustrating how learning cultures can become paralyzed by analysis when reflection loses connection to purpose. Through the recalibration led by Ardent Forward, the firm re-anchored its learning practices in strategic priorities, emphasizing application and impact. The case invites students and leaders to explore how organizations can balance humility with decisiveness, openness with accountability, and continuous learning with sustainable performance in knowledge-intensive environments.

title: Ethical Integration of Generative AI in Hospital Quality Management Systems: A Qualitative Exploration in the Middle East

detail.title: Ethical Integration of Generative AI in Hospital Quality Management Systems: A Qualitative Exploration in the Middle East

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no disclaimers to report.

detail.abstract:
Background: Although integrating generative AI into hospital Quality Management Systems has great potential to improve patient safety and operational effectiveness, it also presents difficult ethical issues with regard to accountability, algorithmic bias, and transparency. There is a critical gap because current ethical frameworks are still more concerned with clinical applications than QMS procedures. This is especially true in the Middle East, where contextspecific guidance is needed due to cultural differences in decision-making norms, fragmented regulations, and heterogeneous healthcare infrastructure. 

Methodology: A qualitative research design was employed. Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted with principal stakeholders in Quality Management and AI as a subspecialty in several Middle Eastern hospitals. Using the ATLAS.ti software, thematic analysis was employed to methodically document and structure patterns of findings relating to the ethical dimensions of concern, barriers to implementation, and responsive actions for the ethical use of GenAI

Key Findings: Prioritizing patient safety (95%) with AI serving as a decision-support tool under human supervision, guaranteeing transparency and informed consent (90%) in the face of regulatory variability, and addressing universal data privacy concerns (100%), such as algorithmic bias and an excessive dependence on automation (60-75%), were among the major themes. In addition, participants supported human-AI cooperation in clinical decision-making (95%), automated documentation (70%), and predictive analytics (80%). 

Conclusion & Implications: The findings underscore the need for a socio-organizational approach to ethical AI integration in Middle Eastern QMS, combining human oversight, transparency, and culturally adaptive strategies. This ensures a balanced, socially responsible framework for AI adoption in healthcare, addressing both ethical controversies and regional specificities.

title: Sectoral Exposure to Heat: Heterogeneous Impacts of Extreme Heat on Workplace Accidents in Italy
affiliations: University of Urbino and University of Urbino Carlo Bo

detail.title: Sectoral Exposure to Heat: Heterogeneous Impacts of Extreme Heat on Workplace Accidents in Italy
detail.abstract: This study examines how extreme heat affects workplace accidents in Italy's various economic sectors. Using granular data by sector, day, and province (NUTS-3) for 2018-2024, we evaluate the contribution of occupational exposure as a source of diverse effects at the sector level. Our findings imply that while the average effects of extreme heat on workplace accidents are, at best, negligible, high temperatures significantly raise the frequency of medium-to-low severity accidents for sectors with high levels of exposure, while exposure and extreme heat alone do not account for fatalities.

title: The Cost of Silence: The Criminalization of Abortion in Botswana — Between Public Morality and Reproductive Rights
affiliations: Gaborone University College of Law and Professional Studies

detail.title: The Cost of Silence: The Criminalization of Abortion in Botswana — Between Public Morality and Reproductive Rights
detail.abstract: This paper explores the criminalization of abortion in Botswana through three intersecting lenses: legal positivism versus natural law, feminist legal theory, and the public health perspective. It makes the case that the strict abortion law in Botswana which are deeply rooted in a misplaced sense of morality, presented as moral conservatism and colonial legal traditions, continue to silence women's reproductive autonomy and rights, thus they continue to perpetuate inequality. The discussion illustrates how the reliance of the state on moral and religious reasoning continues to undermine women's rights and public health outcomes, leading to unsafe abortions and preventable maternal deaths. Ultimately, the paper calls for a rights-based reform of Botswana's abortion laws that harmonizes moral values with constitutional and international human rights obligations. .

title: Consumer Perceptions on Electrical Vehicles in the Indian Market
affiliations: Christ (Deemed to be) University, M S Ramaiah Institute of Management, Christ University Bangalore and T S Mishra University

detail.title: Consumer Perceptions on Electrical Vehicles in the Indian Market
detail.abstract: This study investigates consumer perceptions regarding Electrical Vehicles (EVs) within the Indian market. The research aims to discern the attitudes, preferences, and behavioral intentions of consumers towards EV adoption. It focuses on understanding the factors influencing consumer decision-making processes in embracing EVs over conventional vehicles. Through a meticulous examination and analysis of data collected from diverse demographic segments across India, this study endeavors to quantify the level of consumer awareness, knowledge, and sentiments regarding EVs. It seeks to measure the correlation between these perceptions and various influential factors such as infrastructure readiness, attitudes towards EVs, government policies and incentives, environmental concerns, range anxiety, psychological and economic factors, understanding of EV technologies, and social influences. By delineating the landscape of consumer perceptions and preferences towards EVs in the Indian market, this research aims to provide valuable insights for industry stakeholders, policymakers, and marketers. The outcomes of this study aspire to contribute to the development of strategies and policies aimed at fostering greater EV adoption in India while offering a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities inherent in the EV market landscape.

title: Hydropower Dams, Deforestation, and Land use Change: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca - Department of Economics, Management and Statistics (DEMS) and University of Milan

detail.title: Hydropower Dams, Deforestation, and Land use Change: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: In Brazil, hydropower generates more than 60% of the national electricity supply, placing the country among the most hydropower-dependent economies worldwide. This study analyses the causal impact of dam construction on forest loss in Brazil using a new municipality-level panel dataset covering 379 dams, combined with high-resolution satellite data on forest coverage, among other variables. Applying modern staggered differenceindifferences estimators and a dynamic event study, we find that dams reduce forest cover by almost 9% percent in the municipality. No anticipatory effects are detected, but postconstruction losses increase steadily over time. Mechanism show that forest loss occurs mainly through cropland expansion, with smaller increases in pasture and higher agricultural value added. Effects are concentrated in the North and NorthEast regions, amplified in municipalities with high public land shares and unequal land distribution, consistent with persistent institutional legacies. Our results highlight that while hydropower enhances energy security, it entails substantial environmental costs requiring stronger land governance.

title: Trust, Usefulness, and Dependency on AI in Programming: A Hierarchical Clustering Approach
affiliations: Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University, Don Honorio Ventura State University and

detail.title: Trust, Usefulness, and Dependency on AI in Programming: A Hierarchical Clustering Approach
detail.abstract: While AI tools are transforming programming education, their adoption in underrepresented countries remains insufficiently studied. Understanding students' trust, perceived usefulness, and dependency on AI tools is essential to improving their integration into education. For these purposes, this study surveyed 508 first-year programming students in Pampanga, Philippines and analyzed their perceptions using hierarchical clustering. Results showed four unique student profiles with varying in trust and usage intensity. While students acknowledged AI tools' benefits, dependency remained low due to limited infrastructure and insufficient exposure. Highfrequency users did not necessarily report greater trust or usefulness which may indicates a complex relationship between usage patterns and perception. This study recommends that to maximize AI's educational impact, targeted interventions such as infrastructure development, training programs, and curriculum integration are necessary. This study provides empirical insights to support equitable and effective AI adoption in programming education within developing regions.

title: Weather Shocks and Sectoral Labour Reallocation: Evidence from the European Regions
affiliations: University of Milan - University of Milan, University of Milan - University of Milan and Università degli Studi di Milano

detail.title: Weather Shocks and Sectoral Labour Reallocation: Evidence from the European Regions
detail.abstract: This paper examines how weather variability influences inter-sectoral labour reallocation and sectoral value-added (GVA) growth across 238 European regional units (NUTS2 level) from 1980 to 2022. Leveraging this large and granular dataset, we employ flexible functional forms within a fixed-effects panel framework, where the impact of weather shocks is conditional on long-term climate. Unlike previous empirical research in climate economics, which primarily focused on inter-annual variations in average temperature, this study emphasizes the significant role of daily temperature variability. Temperature variability is particularly critical in warmer regions with low seasonal variability, which are more vulnerable to sudden temperature shifts or rainfall shocks. In hot and low seasonal variability regions-i.e. Mediterranean ones-we find a robust adaptive response of the labour market where workers move from climate-sensitive agriculture to less affected service sector. The heterogeneous effects of weather shocks on sectoral value-added growth appear to be a possible mechanism driving this labour reallocation, although more complex factors may also be at play.

title: Promoting Safe Opioid Disposal: Experimental Evidence on Behavioral Messaging with Financial Incentives
affiliations: University of Warwick, Office of Evaluation Sciences, U.S. General Services Administration, U.S. General Services Administration, University of Pennsylvania, Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), Office of Evaluation Sciences, U.S. General Services Administration, Government of the United States of America - Department of State and Office of Evaluation Sciences, U.S. General Services Administration

detail.title: Promoting Safe Opioid Disposal: Experimental Evidence on Behavioral Messaging with Financial Incentives
detail.abstract: A large proportion of patients prescribed opioid pills fail to properly dispose of their unused pills, posing a risk for others. We designed a field experiment to test reminder cards aimed at increasing the take-up of financial incentives for the secure return of unused pills among Veterans. The reminder cards, which incorporate key principles from behavioral economics, increase the return of unused opioid pills, both at the extensive margin (likelihood of return) and the intensive margin (number returned). Our low-cost behavioral intervention enhances the efficacy of the financial incentive and reduces the per-person and per-pill returned costs.

detail.title: Government Research
detail.abstract:
Legal scholars have long recognized that the patent system is only one tool among many in law and policy for incentivizing innovation. The innovation-law toolkit includes a host of other institutions, most prominently innovation prizes, research-and-development (R&D) tax credits, and government-funded research grants. Scholars have assessed how each of these, like patents, directs R&D resources toward promising projects, motivates strong performance by researchers, and rewards success. Grants loom particularly large in these analyses, as the federal government remains by far the single largest funder of research in the U.S. economy. In the grant system, the government funds research projects that patents often fail to incentivize, and relies on contractors in academia and industry to perform the R&D. 

Conspicuously absent in the innovation-law literature is the role of research conducted by the government itself. The federal government is not only the nation's largest funder of research but also its largest performer. So-called "intramural" R&D conducted by federal agencies, national laboratories, and other government-funded R&D centers comprises a considerable portion-in recent years, close to half-of the government's overall research budget. Given its historical and continuing importance to national innovation efforts, government research should be conceptualized as a distinct paradigm in the innovation-law toolkit. 

In this Article, I provide the first comprehensive analysis of government research from an innovation-law perspective. I outline the basic institutional design of government research and, using case studies of the National Institutes of Health Intramural Research Program and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, show how it works in practice. I then identify a particular niche in which government research has clear comparative advantages: high-risk, high-reward projects that require massive scale, interdisciplinary collaboration, and long-term funding. I also explore normative justifications for government research beyond efficient knowledge production, including the building of state capacity for developmental policy and a more equitable distribution of the gains from innovation. By integrating government research into this broader institutional framework, this Article reaffirms the state's indispensable role in innovation law and policy and reasserts the values that ought to guide its future development.

title: Innovation Policy Feedback
affiliations: Syracuse University - College of Law

detail.title: Innovation Policy Feedback
detail.abstract:
Innovation law scholars have long been interested in how the institutional and administrative design of the U.S. federal research system might be improved. Much of this work has sought to improve efficiency and increase innovative output from federal research agencies, and a second line of scholarship has explored how federal R&D policy can better serve societal goals beyond maximizing innovation. What all this work shares is an assumption––largely implicit––that underlying political support for government-supported research is basically secure.

That assumption no longer holds. For virtually the first time since it came into being, the federal research system is under attack. The second Trump Administration has launched a full-scale assault on the government’s support for science and technology development by cutting R&D funding, firing government researchers, freezing research grants to universities, and threatening immigrant scientists. Where this assault will ultimately leave the research system is unclear. What is certain is that this system is now in crisis. 

This moment calls for a new framework for reforming the federal research system. That framework, I suggest, should put politics first, orienting reforms toward shoring up political support for R&D policy so that the federal research system can rebound from the current crisis and better withstand future hostile administrations. To refocus reform efforts on political design, I draw from the interdisciplinary literature on “policy feedback”––how policies, once enacted, can become self-reinforcing or self-undermining by reshaping political consistencies, state capacities, and mass attitudes.

This Article charts a new course for innovation policy that is more sensitive to the logic of policy feedback. It suggests that federal innovation programs––and the research system as a whole––can and should be designed to mobilize stronger R&D-linked political constituencies, install more resilient internal research capacities in the government, and better convey the importance and material benefits of the research system to the public. Applying this framework, I highlight examples of past research programs with largely positive feedback effects and those with negative feedback effects. I also examine the Biden Administration’s signature R&D bill, the Chips and Science Act, as an example of both. By more carefully considering the feedback loops generated by innovation policies, scholars and policymakers can set the federal research system back on a stronger footing with the potential for even further expansion.

title: CONTROLLED STABILITY MODEL: An Algorithmic Solution Against Expectation Traps, Fiscal Indiscipline, and the Middle-Income Trap in Developing Economies

detail.title: CONTROLLED STABILITY MODEL: An Algorithmic Solution Against Expectation Traps, Fiscal Indiscipline, and the Middle-Income Trap in Developing Economies

keywords: An Algorithmic Solution Against Expectation Traps
and the Middle-Income Trap in Developing Economies

detail.abstract: This study identifies the primary reason developing economies remain stuck in chronic currency crises as economic management succumbing to human frailty (lack of political will, short-term populism) and the instantaneous, emotional expectations of markets. Turkey's 2002-2018 growth period and subsequent vulnerabilities, along with Argentina's recurring crises, demonstrate the devastating consequences of the exchange rate decoupling from physical reserves, the resulting consumption boom financed by debt triggered by an appreciating local currency despite no increase in production, and the hidden inflation tax created by uncontrolled money printing by the state. This situation condemns countries to the Middle-Income Trap. The proposed Controlled Stability Model presents a transparent, algorithm-based framework, independent of political will and human frailty, to overcome this challenge. The model's core premise: "It is impossible for a local currency to appreciate sustainably, enriching the populace, without real foreign exchange inflows; systems enabling this (purely through expectations) are doomed to fail." By mathematically pegging the currency's value to physical foreign exchange reserves, the model neutralizes emotional expectations and physically prevents the government from printing money arbitrarily. The model's bilateral ±15% exchange rate fluctuation limit controls both value loss during crises and value appreciation during excessive foreign exchange inflows, thereby curbing domestic inflation and promoting income equality. In case of a liquidity crisis, the system triggers a controlled economic cooling process. The model's Insured Deposit System breaks the crisis expectation cycle. This controlled cooling process serves as a national development strategy by forcing domestic industry (including intermediate goods) to strengthen and creating an "economic shell" that enhances resilience after each crisis. Ultimately, the model compels the state towards fiscal discipline, preventing the erosion of public wealth through hidden taxes.

title: Beyond Geographical Localization: Individual Determinants of Knowledge Spillover Absorption in Inventors

detail.title: Beyond Geographical Localization: Individual Determinants of Knowledge Spillover Absorption in Inventors
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper examines how individual-level characteristics shape inventors' ability to absorb knowledge spillovers. While prior research has focused on firm-or regional-level determinants, this study investigates the micro-foundations of spillover absorption by analyzing how education, experience breadth, and mobility jointly influence knowledge diffusion. 

Methodology: Using inventor-level data from the PatVal-EU survey covering 6,327 inventors in six European countries, a series of binary probit models estimates the probability of absorbing near and distant knowledge spillovers. Three hypotheses are tested on the influence of labor mobility, knowledge breadth, and depth on knowledge spillover absorption. Six model specifications separately and jointly assess these effects.

Findings: Results show that interregional mobility significantly increases the probability of absorbing knowledge spillovers, while intra-regional or residential mobility has a limited influence. Education depth positively affects spillover absorption up to the Master's level, but PhD education yields no additional benefit, suggesting diminishing returns to knowledge depth. The Herfindahl Index of experience concentration is negative and significant, indicating that broader technological experience enhances absorptive ability. Contrary to the hypothesized inverted-U pattern, knowledge breadth positively linearly affects spillover absorption. The results confirm that mobility and absorptive capacity complement each other, helping individuals internalize knowledge from geographically.

Unique contribution to theory, practice and policy: The study extends absorptive capacity theory to the individual level, demonstrating that education, cognitive diversity, and mobility jointly determine spillover absorption. It contributes to innovation policy and practice by emphasizing the benefits of promoting interregional mobility and the importance of both depth and breadth of knowledge.

title: Do multicultural barriers hinder fintech development A pre-registered report
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics, University of International Business and Economics and University of International Business and Economics

detail.title: Do multicultural barriers hinder fintech development A pre-registered report
detail.abstract: This pre-registered report aims to explore the impact of cultural diversity on fintech development through the perspective of dialectal diversity. Specifically, we want to investigate three key questions: (1) Does cultural diversity influence fintech development? (2) If it does, what are the underlying mechanisms? (3) Moreover, does the impact of cultural diversity on fintech development vary across regions or households with heterogeneous characteristics? To explore these questions, we plan to utilize regional dialect data and analytical methods such as instrumental variables and fixed effects to examine fintech adoption at the household level. This report contributes to understanding the informal institutional factors underpinning the development of  fintech, and provides new theoretical and practical perspectives for building a more comprehensive and inclusive fintech system.

title: The Theory of Adversarial Asset Pricing
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: The Theory of Adversarial Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: This paper develops a general theory of adversarial pricing, a unified framework for derivative valuation under model uncertainty, market frictions, and strategic interaction. Building on the observation that the classical risk-neutral measure arises as Nature's optimal mixed strategy in a dynamic hedger-Nature game, we generalise the Black-Scholes world to zero-sum stochastic differential games in which both the trader and the market choose controls. The Isaacs condition of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equation corresponds to the existence of an equilibrium measure. Extensions cover uncertain volatility, jumps, transaction costs, and calibration constraints, providing tight, consistent bounds for exotic options. We further extend the theory of adversarial pricing to path-dependent derivatives, including barrier, lookback, and other exotic options. The underlying market is modelled as a two-player zero-sum stochastic differential game between a hedger and an adversarial Nature controlling volatility, jumps, and barriers consistent with the observed vanilla smile. The value function is characterised by a fully nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs variational inequality. We derive existence and comparison results, discuss numerical schemes, and illustrate the resulting bid-ask bounds under volatility and frictional uncertainty.

title: Cooperation and Willingness to Pay in Rare Diseases: Survey Evidence from GNE Myopathy Patients
affiliations: Jindal Global Law School, Jindal Global Business School and University of Bologna - Department of Economics

detail.title: Cooperation and Willingness to Pay in Rare Diseases: Survey Evidence from GNE Myopathy Patients
detail.abstract: Rare diseases affect small patient populations and often lack effective treatments, prompting some patients to actively support drug research and development. This study examines the determinants of patients' willingness to pay (WTP) and willingness to contribute effort for treatment development in the context of GNE myopathy, a progressive, rare neuromuscular disorder. Using survey data from 50 patients and six interviews with patient advocates, we analyze how different socioeconomic factors including income, disease severity, family support, trust, community engagement, and perceptions of collective behavior shape both monetary and non-monetary contributions. Results show that income is the strongest and most consistent predictor of WTP, while social trust and community connectedness act as key non-monetary drivers. Individuals in more advanced disease stages exhibit higher WTP for a onetime curative treatment, whereas those with stronger family support show significantly lower willingness to fund research. Willingness to exert non-monetary effort correlates positively with optimism about future treatment availability, engagement in the GNE community, and awareness of patient organizations. In contrast with community advocates, patients, though prosocial, contribute small proportions of their income and place less emphasis on the scientific process of treatment development. Financial constraints, information opacity, and institutional weaknesses-rather than solidarity-emerge as primary barriers to collective action. These findings highlight that governments need to work with community advocates to reduce information frictions, foster transparency and encourage funding mechanisms for treatment development.

title: AI and Internal Audit Quality

detail.title: AI and Internal Audit Quality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest in regards to this study.

detail.abstract: The internal audit function plays a critical role in providing assurance over governance, risk management and internal controls. In recent years, artificial intelligence technologies (including machine learning, natural-language processing, and advanced analytics) have been introduced into internal audit processes. This paper examines whether AI strengthens or weakens internal audit quality. On one side, AI offers significant potential benefits including enhanced efficiency, improved data-analytics capability, richer risk-identification, continuous monitoring, and higher coverage of audit areas. On the other side, AI also introduces risks and challenges such as data-quality issues, algorithmic bias, loss of auditor judgment, transparency and explainability concerns, tool dependence, and organizational governance weakness. Through review of recent articles, the paper argues that AI has the potential to strengthen internal audit quality, but only if appropriate controls and governance are in place. Otherwise, AI may weaken audit quality and introduce new types of audit risk.

detail.abstract: This study used JKS Granger non-causality and 3SLS to examine causal interactions among tourism arrivals, environmental pollution and health outcomes in Africa. The causality perspective revealed a Granger-caused relationship between tourism arrivals, environmental pollution, and health outcomes. The results from 3SLS indicated that tourism is positively linked with health outcomes and environmental pollution, while tourism and health outcomes are also positively related to environmental pollution. Given our findings, prioritising sustainable tourism should be the government's priority.

title: Who Decides? The Role of Parental Rights in Abortion and Gender-Affirming-Care Decisions for Minors
affiliations: Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law

detail.title: Who Decides? The Role of Parental Rights in Abortion and Gender-Affirming-Care Decisions for Minors

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 713
publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The American legal system presumes that children’s interests are best protected by their parents and, secondarily, by the state’s parens patriae authority. Yet this structure falters when parental authority and state power are infused with political and ideological agendas. This Essay examines how these dynamics have distorted decision-making authority in two contexts—minors’ access to abortion and gender-affirming medical care—and allowed children’s welfare and autonomy to be sacrificed to partisan aims. The law is inconsistent on the role of parental rights—typically empowering parents to grant or withhold consent to a minor’s abortion but categorically stripping them of the power to consent to gender-affirming care for a minor. This inconsistency exposes “parental rights” as a selectively invoked political tool rather than a stable legal principle. Moreover, even a consistent approach to parental rights and decision-making for minors would likely fail to account sufficiently for the unique, lifelong consequences of denying access to abortion or gender-affirming care.

Part I situates these departures within the broader legal framework governing conflicts among parents, children, and the state, illustrating how minors’ interests rarely prevail absent independent constitutional protection or statutory intervention. Part II explores how abortion and gender-affirming care laws have been shaped less by coherent doctrine than by partisan ideology, resulting in idiosyncratic approaches to these particular decisions with the potential for lasting harmful consequences. Part III argues that while fidelity to conventional principles would represent an improvement, at least with respect to gender-affirming care decisions, those principles may simply be inadequate to safeguard children’s autonomy in life-altering decisions. The Essay concludes by urging reconsideration of how the legal system conceptualizes minors’ self-determination, pro-posing that more attention be paid to how decisions might affect children’s well-being than to who has the right to make them.

title: Brazil's Dual VAT (IBS/CBS): Accounting Design, International Comparability, and Implications for Financial Reporting
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research and FUCAPE Business School

detail.title: Brazil's Dual VAT (IBS/CBS): Accounting Design, International Comparability, and Implications for Financial Reporting
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the accounting and financial reporting implications of Brazil's new dual value-added tax system, composed of the state/municipal IBS and the federal CBS. Although rooted in Brazil's tax reform, the system introduces features that are globally relevant, particularly for countries examining VAT modernization and IFRS convergence. The study provides a comparative legal-accounting analysis showing how the mandatory "outside" taxation framework aligns Brazil with international VAT practice, notably in Portugal, Germany, France, and Spain. Consistent with IFRS 15/CPC 47, IBS and CBS are excluded from revenue and expenses, functioning strictly as balance-sheet items (tax receivable or payable). The paper examines consequences for income statements, balance-sheet structures, margin indicators, covenants, and working-capital management. A distinctive innovation of the Brazilian model-the requirement that credit entitlement depends on proof of tax payment in the previous stagecreates timing effects absent in most European VAT systems and shapes companies' cash-flow dynamics during the transition. The paper also evaluates the implications for corporate income tax under both the Actual Profit (Lucro Real) and Presumed Profit regimes, emphasizing the elimination of "tax-on-tax" effects and the expected increase in informational neutrality. Overall, the dual VAT represents a significant step toward international comparability, enhances transparency in financial reporting, and introduces a unique mix of VAT standardization with advanced compliance tools such as split payment.

title: Flipping A Coin For Copyrightability Of Illegally Placed Street Art
affiliations: Lund University

detail.title: Flipping A Coin For Copyrightability Of Illegally Placed Street Art
detail.abstract: Street art is visual art usually placed in public locations, such as on buildings or train cars. Once upon a time, this concept was being treated very stringently within the borders of criminal law. So that, graffiti used to be scrutinised as criminal behaviour or vandalism. We all know how the "Subway Surfers" game starts, do not we? However, tables have turned, and graffitti are now under the umbrella of a concept called an artstreet art. Even discussions were commenced on the copyrightability of street art. The uprising role of this concept took this debate to another level, granting copyright protection to even illegally placed street art. But the runner in "Subway Surfers" still runs because the act of painting surfaces unsolicitedly is still considered illegal. That is why granting copyright protection for illegally placed street art is controversial, especially when the "unclean hands" doctrine is on the other side of the scale. Furthermore, if illegally placed street art gets copyright protection, the discussions will potentially extend to what economic and moral rights street artists can have. This article will address the issues of copyright protection for street art (both legally and illegally placed) and the potential economic and moral rights of street artists.

Therefore, the main object of the study was child labor in sociological, historical, regulatory aspects and its presence on the labor market, and the purpose of the article is to analyze the causes and consequences of attracting minors to work on market conditions, as well as the demand for workers over the age of 14 in the modern Russian labor market.

title: Immigration and the Supreme Court in the Early Days of the Second Trump Administration
affiliations: University of California, Davis - School of Law

detail.title: Immigration and the Supreme Court in the Early Days of the Second Trump Administration

publicationDetails.detailsText: UC Davis Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Davis School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: St. Louis University Law Journal (forthcoming 2026) (Childress Lecture)

detail.abstract:
This paper is a lightly footnoted version on my Dean Richard J. Childress Memorial Lecture at St. Louis University School of Law in October 2025.  

With the inauguration of President Trump for his second term in January 2025, the first nine months of 2025 saw a series of unprecedented immigration enforcement operations.  Unlike anything seen in modern U.S. history, the actions have no less than shocked many observers, me included.  The immigration measures go far above and beyond those pursued in President Trump’s first term in office, which were aggressive themselves.  The centerpiece of the President’s dizzying array of immigration enforcement operations in 2025 is what he has proclaimed to be a mass deportation campaign targeting the “worst of the worst” criminal noncitizens. 

The Supreme Court has been asked to review the lawfulness of many of the administration’s immigration actions, including some cases requiring quick action and placed on the Court’s emergency, or shadow, docket (with limited briefing and oral arguments).  It responded in several instances with short opinions.  Consistent with the Court’s historical treatment of immigration matters, the Court’s rulings have been mixed, with the administration winning some cases and losing others.  This paper analyzes the Court's immigration rulings in the early days of President Trump's second term.

title: Интерактивные оценки технологий как инклюзивные формы управления технологическим развитием (Interactive Technology Assessment as Inclusive Form of Governance of Technological Development)
affiliations: Russian Academy of National Economy and Public Administration under the President of the Russian Federation (RANEPA) - North-West Institute of Management

detail.title: Интерактивные оценки технологий как инклюзивные формы управления технологическим развитием (Interactive Technology Assessment as Inclusive Form of Governance of Technological Development)
detail.abstract:
Russian Abstract: В статье рассматривается группа особых подходов к оценке технологий, которая получила название интерактивных мето- дов. В современных условиях имеется ряд предпосылок к раз- витию и применению данных методов оценивания: требования развивающейся демократии, сложный характер воздействия многих инновационных технологий, культурный плюрализм со- временного общества и другие. Интерактивные методы имеют обширные цели: оценка различных рисков, выяснение отноше- ния общества к той или иной инновации, прояснение возмож- ных конфликтов, содействие разработке взвешенной техно- логической политики. Оценка технологий может проводиться в разных вариантах. Так, в статье проводится различие оценки технологий в сильном и слабом смысле. Отмечается, что ин- терактивные методы имеют определенные недостатки. Кри- тически важным является адекватное использование лицами, принимающими решения, результатов интерактивной оценки.

English Abstract: The article discusses a group of special approaches to technology assessment, which is called interactive methods. In modern conditions, there are a number of prerequisites for the development and application of these assessment methods: the requirements of a developing democracy, the complex nature of the impact of many innovative technologies, the cultural pluralism of modern society, and others. Interactive methods have broad goals: evaluating various risks, exploring society’s attitude to a particular innovation, clarifying possible conflicts, and facilitating the development of a balanced technology policy. Technology assessment can be carried out in different ways. Thus, the article distinguishes technology assessment in a strong and weak sense. It is noted that interactive methods have certain disadvantages. It is critically important that decision makers make adequate use of the results of the interactive assessment.

title: Эмерджентные формы открытого управления (open governance) как новые тенденции общественного участия в решении проблем городского управления (Emergent forms of open governance as new trends in public participation in solving urban governance problems)
affiliations: Russian Academy of National Economy and Public Administration under the President of the Russian Federation (RANEPA) - North-West Institute of Management

detail.title: Эмерджентные формы открытого управления (open governance) как новые тенденции общественного участия в решении проблем городского управления (Emergent forms of open governance as new trends in public participation in solving urban governance problems)
detail.abstract:
Russian Abstract: В статье рассматриваются проблемы становления новых форм публичного управления, связанных с возможностями, которые обеспечивают для гражданского участия новые информационные технологии. Эти формы подпадают под широкое понятие открытого управления, которое сегодня активно обсуждается с научной и практической точек зрения. Приводимые в статье примеры показывают, что данные формы обладают такими характеристиками, как эмерджентность, самоорганизация и массовое участие, а также демонстрируют такой общий паттерн, как формирование единого открытого оперативноинформационного пространства с неограниченным количеством участников. Обсуждается вопрос о том, можно ли считать эти тенденции началом формирования отдельной управленческой парадигмы. В статье рассматриваются вопросы дальнейшего расширения и развития подхода открытого управления для решения напряженных общественных проблем. Ключевые слова: открытое управление, открытое правительство, цифровизация управления, публичное управление, информационное общество, участие общественности.

English Abstract: The article discusses the problems of the formation new forms of public governance related to the opportunities provided by new information technologies for civil participation. These forms fall under the broad concept of open governance, which is currently being actively discussed from a scientific and practical perspective. The examples provided in the article show that these forms have such characteristics as emergence, self-organization, and mass participation, and also demonstrate a common pattern of forming an integrated open operational and information space with an unlimited number of participants. The article discusses whether these trends can be considered the beginning of a new governance paradigm. It explores the potential for further expansion and development of open governance approaches to address pressing societal challenges.

title: The Housing Market in China: An Estimated DSGE Model

detail.title: The Housing Market in China: An Estimated DSGE Model
detail.abstract: This study develops a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model incorporating housing, banking, and government sectors, with a focus on the role of dynamic land prices in China's economy. The model is calibrated using Chinese macroeconomic data and demonstrates a strong fit with observed business cycle fluctuations. Through shock decomposition analysis, we identify capital shocks, housing supply shocks, and housing demand shocks as the primary drivers of variations in consumption, investment, loans, and house prices. Impulse response analysis reveals that the banking sector amplifies economic shocks, while local government activities-acting as the dominant land supplier-crowd out household consumption and significantly influence macroeconomic dynamics. Furthermore, welfare analysis shows that government control over land reduces overall social welfare, whereas the presence of the banking sector enhances it. The model offers a new DSGE benchmark for China's business cycle analysis.

detail.abstract: I develop a novel online experiment with 387 subjects on Prolific and simple utility model to examine how workers respond to reported work meaning. Workers appear to value different aspects of work and be willing to give up other incentives for their best work match. 31% of workers appear not to value meaning in their work, 27% appear not to value work pay, 30% appear to value both, and 12% cannot be characterized. Overall, 57% of workers are willing to sacrifice up to 14% of possible pay in their pursuit of meaningful work. For workers who value work meaning, I estimate positive impacts of meaningfulness on the quantity and quality of output, although these effects appear only for a task with prosocial framing. Finally, I validate a light-touch treatment designed to increase worker awareness of the value they place on meaning, again finding effects only for workers who seek meaning in their work. Importantly, raising worker awareness of work meaning has no impact on the types of incentives they seek out. These results offer insights into how such interventions and preferences for work meaning might be leveraged in organizational settings.

title: Correcting Second-Order Beliefs across the Political Divide: Experimental Evidence on Climate Change Beliefs

detail.title: Correcting Second-Order Beliefs across the Political Divide: Experimental Evidence on Climate Change Beliefs
detail.abstract: Misperceptions of what others think are widespread and shape how individuals form their own beliefs and take actions. On polarizing issues, the effect of correcting these misperceptions may depend on political affiliation. I examine this through a preregistered online experiment on climate change beliefs, a highly polarized issue in the United States. Using incentive-compatible methods, I elicit participants’ own beliefs and their beliefs about others’ beliefs (second-order beliefs). I then provide randomized information about others’ actual beliefs from either a co-partisan or an opposing partisan source, and observe the updated beliefs and pro-climate actions. I find that correcting misperceptions in second-order beliefs affects one’s own beliefs and actions about climate change, and the effects depend on whether the individual and the information source are politically aligned. Stronger pro-climate beliefs from co-partisans increase individuals’ own pro-climate beliefs and behaviors, while identical information from opposing partisans generates backlash. These results suggest that uniform social information campaigns may have a limited impact on polarized issues, while tailoring messages to match the audience’s political affiliation offers a more promising strategy for improving engagement.

detail.abstract: This report analyzes two and a half decades of global macroeconomic data to forecast the direction of global growth, trade, inflation, and financial stability in 2026. Drawing from multilateral sources including the IMF, World Bank, WTO, and BIS, the analysis highlights a cautiously stable world economy expected to expand around 3.1 percent. Structural forces-aging demographics, artificial intelligence capital expenditure, the energy transition, and fragmented industrial policies-shape this outlook. The findings underline the need for portfolio strategies emphasizing diversification, balance sheet strength, and exposure to long-term technological trends.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the profound influence of short-form video consumption on the financial decision making patterns of young investors in India. As digital platforms increasingly permeate daily life, concerns arise regarding their impact on cognitive functions essential for sound financial planning. This research aims to understand how habits formed through engaging with rapid, dopamine-driven content might alter attention spans, patience, and risk perception, subsequently affecting saving behaviors, investment choices, and overall financial discipline. A mixed-methods approach, primarily utilizing surveys combined with hypothetical financial scenarios, was employed with a sample of young Indian investors aged 18 to 35. Preliminary findings suggest a discernible correlation between higher short-form video engagement and a preference for immediate gratification, reduced long-term financial planning, and a potential inclination towards speculative investments. The study highlights an emerging challenge in nurturing financially astute generations and underscores the need for conscious digital consumption and targeted financial literacy initiatives.

title: Computation as a Game
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Computation as a Game
detail.abstract: We present a unifying representation of computation as a two-player game between an Algorithm and Nature, grounded in domain theory and game theory. The Algorithm produces progressively refined approximations within a Scott domain, while Nature assigns penalties proportional to their distance from the true value. Correctness corresponds to equilibrium in the limit of refinement. This framework allows us to define complexity classes game-theoretically, characterizing P, NP, and related classes as sets of problems admitting particular equilibria. The open question P ? = NP becomes a problem about the equivalence of Nash equilibria under differing informational and temporal constraints. We then extend the game-theoretic interpretation of computation into a probabilistic and collective setting, formulating a mean-field theory of computation. Each individual computation is modeled as a stochastic process on a domain, interacting weakly with the aggregate distribution of other computations. We derive equilibrium conditions analogous to those of mean-field games and interpret complexity classes in terms of the structure and stability of these equilibria. The P vs. NP question thus becomes a question of whether deterministic mean-field equilibria can approximate their existentially quantified counterparts in the large-population limit. Finally, we present a categorical formulation of the game-theoretic theory of computation. In this view, programs are morphisms in a cartesian closed category, computational refinement corresponds to the internal order in a domain object, and equilibria are fixed points of endofunctors representing interaction between an Algorithm and Nature. Complexity classes arise as subcategories defined by resource-bounded morphisms. The question P ? = NP becomes the question of whether two endofunctors-deterministic and existential-are isomorphic in the topos of feasible computations.

title: Трансдисциплинарные проекты городского развития: сущность и основные проблемы (Transdisciplinary Urban Development Projects: The Essence and Main Problems)

detail.abstract:
Russian Abstract: Трансдисциплинарные исследования и разработки все шире применяются в настоящее время для решения проблем город- ского управления и развития. В статье рассматривается сущ- ность трансдисциплинарного подхода, приводятся его опре- деления и основные характеристики. Обсуждаются типичные сложности данного подхода (трудоемкость, трудности прео- доления дисциплинарных границ и интеграции знаний и т.п.). В связи с этим в статье предлагается более реалистичный подход, включающий умеренные начальные цели и установки исследования, не предполагающие обязательного преодоле- ния дисциплинарных границ и получения радикально нового знания. При этом само планирование трансдисциплинарного исследования должно сопровождаться тщательным обоснова- нием выбора данной формы взаимодействия участников. Уме- ренная исходная установка проекта может далее трансформи- роваться в более сильный вариант в процессе развертывания самой логики разработки решаемой проблемы.

English Abstract: Transdisciplinary research and development is increasingly being applied to address urban governance and development issues. The article examines the essence of the transdisciplinary approach, provides its definitions and main characteristics. The typical difficulties of this approach (labor intensity, difficulties in overcoming disciplinary boundaries and integrating knowledge, etc.) are discussed. In this regard, the article suggests a more realistic approach, including moderate initial goals and research objectives that do not necessarily involve overcoming disciplinary boundaries and obtaining radically new knowledge. At the same time, the planning of transdisciplinary research itself should be accompanied by a thorough justification of the choice of this form of interaction between the participants. The moderate initial setup of the project can further transform into a stronger version in the process of deploying the very logic of developing the problem being solved.

detail.abstract: This paper extends the Systemic Risk of Doing Business (SRDB) inflation framework by modeling timevarying component weights w j,t that evolve according to economic cycle theory and convergence dynamics. Prior work assumed constant weights (w 1 , w 2 , w 3) = (0.24, 0.57, 0.19) derived via GMM. We demonstrate that weights evolve systematically over economic cycles and across development stages. Key Results: (1) Financial risk weight w 2 varies 0.42-0.71 over Kondratiev long-wave cycle (40-60 years), peaking during downswings (2008-20: 0.71, +34% vs average). (2) Computational cost weight w 1 varies 0.18-0.32 over Juglar medium-cycle (7-11 years), peaking during credit booms (+78% swing). (3) All three weights exhibit β-convergence (β < 0, p < 0.01) with half-lives 22-38 years. (4) Crosscountry weight dispersion declines σ = 0.18 (1970) → 0.08 (2020)-σ-convergence confirmed (56% reduction). (5) Emerging economies weight structural fragility 0.30 vs advanced 0.16; advanced economies weight financial risk 0.62 vs emerging 0.42. (6) Markov-switching identifies 4 K-wave phases; SRDB transmission elasticity γ ranges 0.68-0.92 across regimes. (7) Time-varying weights improve RMSE 18.6% (average), 24.4% (Markov-switching), 44% (crisis periods). (8) State-space Kalman filter with time-varying parameters outperforms fixed-weight specification on all metrics. Methodological Contributions: (1) Integration of three economic cycle theories (Kondratiev, Juglar, Kitchin) with inflation dynamics. (2) Convergence analysis (15 countries, 1960-2025) showing institutional and development determinants of weight evolution. (3) State-space model with exogenous cycle indicators and convergence drivers. (4) Hamilton Markov-switching regime identification matching historical K-wave phases. (5) Complete appendices with country-specific results (15 nations), Kondratiev wave dating, Kalman filter algorithm, and Markov-switching EM procedure. Policy Implications: Central banks should adjust SRDB component emphasis based on cycle phase (financial stress dominates during K-wave downswings; computational stress during Juglar booms) and development stage (structural fragility priority for emerging economies). Forecasting gains of 44% during crises demonstrate practical value.

title: How Middle Powers May Prevent the Development of Artificial Superintelligence
affiliations: , Conjecture, Control AI and Conjecture

detail.title: How Middle Powers May Prevent the Development of Artificial Superintelligence
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) development, and especially the pursuit of artificial superintelligence (ASI), presents unprecedented risks to international security, potentially enabling any actor who develops it first to achieve decisive strategic advantage over all others; alternatively, it may result in humanity's extinction if humanity loses control of a powerful AI system. Middle powers are particularly well-incentivized to kickstart international coordination aimed at preventing the development of ASI by any actor. In this work, we propose an international agreement which would enable a coalition of middle powers to deter dangerous AI R&D and eventually achieve a regime of international coordination in which AI R&D is restricted and thoroughly monitored in order to prevent the development of ASI. The agreement establishes this deterrence through clearly defined AI R&D redlines tied to specific, graduated countermeasures. These measures range from export controls, through various levels of sanctions, and culminate in the recognition of self-defense rights when the most egregiously dangerous redlines are breached. Member states must commit to escalating deterrence measures in unison; this way, they may meaningfully deter dangerous AI R&D by any actor, including superpowers. The effectiveness of this initiative critically depends on timing. Once actors are confident that they may achieve decisive strategic advantage through AI R&D, they may be willing to endure extraordinary costs as a temporary price for permanent global dominance; earlier implementation can achieve the agreement's goals without resorting to extreme measures.

title: Riemannian Manifolds of Asymmetric Equilibria: The Victoria-Nash Geometry
affiliations: Royal Statistical Society

detail.title: Riemannian Manifolds of Asymmetric Equilibria: The Victoria-Nash Geometry
detail.abstract: We introduce the Victoria-Nash manifold Γ V N AE (θ) as a smooth submanifold arising from an asymmetric expectation field F (s; θ). With a Riemannian metric g(θ) and curvature K(s; θ) encoding asymmetry via a smooth structural field ϕ(s; θ), Γ V N AE generalizes Nash equilibria, von Neumann's minimax theory, and Lyapunov stability. We prove existence, smoothness, and invariance using Lefschetz, Tikhonov, and Lyapunov-Morse theory. Classical equilibria are degenerate limits under complete symmetry and vanishing curvature.

title: When Nature Turns Hazy: How Wildfire Smoke Affects Outdoor Recreation
